blocks.text: **UNIX** is a **multi-user, multitasking** operating system. Its development began in **1969** at **AT&T Bell Laboratories**. The principal developers were **Ken Thompson** and **Dennis Ritchie**; in exam questions Ken Thompson is often called the **father of UNIX**.

blocks.title: UNIX at a glance
items: Development starts at AT&T Bell Laboratories
DEC PDP-7 minicomputer ran the first implementation
Early UNIX was written in assembly language
Much of UNIX was rewritten in the C language

blocks.title: How UNIX's code evolved
items: Rewritten so it is easy to port

blocks.title: Key points
rows: C made UNIX easier to port to different hardware; C's early development was closely linked to UNIX system programming
**UNICS**, commonly expanded as 'Uniplexed Information and Computing Service' - later became UNIX

blocks.text: **Portability** was a major reason for UNIX's spread. Remember the chain: Bell Labs (1969), Thompson and Ritchie, PDP-7, assembly, then C.

blocks.title: Key features
rows: Several users share the system resources
CPU time is shared among tasks and users
Software can be adapted across computer architectures
Directories form a tree that starts at the root /
User accounts, ownership and access permissions
Strong networking facilities; valued for stability and reliability

blocks.title: User interface
rows: **Command-Line Interface** - commands and scripts are typed into a shell

blocks.text: Traditional UNIX interaction is text-based, but graphical environments are also available.

blocks.title: Four-layer view of UNIX
items: Core that manages resources and hardware

blocks.title: The parts explained
rows: Physical CPU, memory, disks, terminals, printers and other devices
The OS core; manages resources and interacts with hardware
Interprets user commands and starts programs
Outer software layer for user tasks

blocks.title: What the kernel does
items: Controls **process scheduling**, memory, devices and file-system services.
Uses **device drivers** to communicate with hardware.
Programs request kernel services through **system calls**.

blocks.title: Three or four?
blocks.text: Counting the hardware gives a **four-layer** view. Counting software only, UNIX has **three main parts**: kernel, shell and utilities/applications. Core = **kernel**; command interpreter = **shell**.

The **root directory** is written **/** and is the top of the directory tree. Directories hold files and subdirectories. Common top-level directories include **bin, etc, home, usr and var**. Applications run as **processes**, and the kernel manages their resources. The shell supports **scripts, pipelines and input/output redirection**.

blocks.title: 'Everything is a file'
blocks.text: This UNIX design principle means many resources, including devices, use **file-like interfaces**. It is not a literal rule for every system object.

blocks.title: The three basic permissions
rows: Add or remove entries where permitted

items: Permissions are assigned separately to the **owner**, the **group** and **others**.
Example: **chmod u+x script.sh** adds execute permission for the owner.

sections.title: UNIX families: System III/V and BSD

blocks.title: Historical branches
rows: Historical AT&T UNIX releases and families
**Berkeley Software Distribution** - originated at the University of California, Berkeley; informally called Berkeley UNIX

blocks.title: BSD contributions
items: The **vi** text editor and the **C shell (csh)** are associated with Berkeley's UNIX work.

blocks.title: BSD descendants
rows: Open-source BSD descendant known for portability; its name is not a standard acronym expansion
Open-source BSD descendant focused on security and code correctness

blocks.text: BSD descendants have genuine historical **UNIX ancestry**; they are not merely inspired by UNIX's design.

blocks.title: Commercial UNIX variants
rows: Originally from **Sun Microsystems**; widely used on Sun workstations and servers, including in the 1990s. Oracle acquired Sun in 2010
Historical **Microsoft** UNIX variant based on licensed UNIX

blocks.title: Modern and related systems
rows: Apple's Mac operating system with BSD and NeXTSTEP heritage; specific releases and configurations have UNIX certification
Independently developed open-source **UNIX-like** kernel used in complete OS distributions; **not derived from original UNIX source**
Linux kernel plus GNU components and other software
'GNU's Not Unix' - this expands GNU, not GNU/Linux

blocks.title: Licensing and certification
blocks.text: Historical AT&T UNIX was **proprietary**; commercial UNIX and open-source UNIX-related systems coexist. **UNIX certification** and **open-source licensing** are different ideas. **Windows 11** belongs to the Windows NT family - it is not UNIX.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: Company to system: **S**un - Solaris, **I**BM - AIX, **H**P - HP-UX, **A**pple - macOS, **M**icrosoft - Xenix, Berkeley - BSD.

sections.title: Commands: general tools, users and logins

blocks.title: General tools
rows: Opens reference manual pages (example: man ls)
Shows previous commands in shells that support it
Displays the system date and time
Pauses execution for a specified time (example: sleep 5)
Shows how long the system has been running, usually with other status data
Writes text or values to standard output (example: echo "Hello UNIX")

blocks.title: Users and logins
rows: Shows the username of the effective user ID
Changes an account password, subject to permissions and policy
Displays recorded login sessions where supported and available

blocks.title: Exam distinctions
blocks.text: **whoami** = effective username. **who** = current login sessions. **last** = recorded login history. **history** = previous shell commands. Command availability and options vary across UNIX/Linux systems.

rows: Print working directory - shows the current directory path

blocks.title: Example session
items: pwd - shows where you are now.
mkdir practice - creates a directory named practice.

blocks.text: **pwd** = Where am I? **cd** = Go elsewhere. **ls** = What is here? **mkdir** = Make folder. **rmdir** = Remove an empty folder.

sections.title: Commands: files, text tools and pipes

blocks.title: File operations
rows: Copies files; suitable options copy directories
Moves or renames files and directories
Removes files; removing directories needs suitable options

blocks.title: Text tools
rows: Reads files and writes their contents in sequence to standard output; can concatenate files
Selects lines that match a given pattern

blocks.title: Worked examples
rows: Adds execute permission for the owner
Joins both files' contents to standard output

blocks.title: The pipe symbol
rows: Connects commands: standard output of the left command becomes standard input of the right command
cat supplies the file contents; grep selects the matching lines

blocks.title: Network commands
rows: Displays or configures network interfaces on systems that provide it
Sends ICMP echo requests to test reachability
Shows connections, routing or interface statistics, depending on options

blocks.text: A failed **ping** does not always mean a host is offline - ICMP traffic may be blocked.

blocks.title: Processes and system control
rows: Lists processes (shows PID, TTY and command)
Sends a signal to a process; commonly requests termination, but the result depends on the signal and how the process handles it
Arranges a controlled shutdown; options may request halt, power-off or restart
Requests that the system stop running

blocks.text: **kill** does not always force an immediate stop. **halt** and **reboot** are not inherently ungraceful - normal operation on many systems includes orderly service shutdown; forced options can change the behaviour.

blocks.title: Quick recall
blocks.text: pwd = current path, mkdir = create directory, rmdir = remove empty directory, cat = display text, grep = search text, chmod = permissions, chown = ownership, mv = move or rename, | = pipe.

revision: UNIX origin: AT&T Bell Laboratories, 1969; developers Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie.
First UNIX ran on a DEC PDP-7 minicomputer, written in assembly; largely rewritten in C in 1973.
UNIX is multi-user, multitasking and time-sharing; portability helped it spread.
Early name UNICS = Uniplexed Information and Computing Service.
CLI = Command-Line Interface; CUI = Character User Interface.
Core of UNIX = kernel; command interpreter = shell; root directory = /.
Permissions r, w, x for owner, group and others; chmod changes them, chown changes ownership.
BSD = Berkeley Software Distribution; vi editor and C shell are linked with Berkeley.
FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD are BSD descendants; Linux is UNIX-like, not derived from UNIX source.
Solaris = Sun, AIX = IBM, HP-UX = Hewlett-Packard, Xenix = Microsoft, IRIX = Silicon Graphics.
GNU = GNU's Not Unix; Windows 11 is in the Windows NT family, not UNIX.
whoami = effective user, who = current logins, last = login history, history = past commands.
pwd shows the path, cd changes directory, ls lists, mkdir creates, rmdir removes an empty directory.
cp copies, mv moves or renames, rm removes, cat displays or joins files, grep searches text.
Pipe | sends the output of the left command to the input of the right command.
ping tests reachability, ifconfig shows interfaces, netstat shows connections, ps shows processes, kill sends a signal.
